sections.title: How does the Cylindrical coordinates calculator work?
sections.html:
The Cylindrical coordinates calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports z (Cylindrical (ρ, θ, z) to Cartesian (x, y, z)) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the x (Cartesian (x, y, z) to cylindrical (ρ, θ, z)), the y (Cartesian (x, y, z) to cylindrical (ρ, θ, z)), the z (Cartesian (x, y, z) to cylindrical (ρ, θ, z)) and the z (Cylindrical (ρ, θ, z) to Cartesian (x, y, z)).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Cylindrical coordinates calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Z=Z
Radius (ρ)=Y ÷ the sine of (Θ)
Radius (ρ)=X ÷ the cosine of (Θ)
Radius (ρ)=the square root of ((X ^ 2) + (Y ^ 2))
Θ=(Y ÷ X)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose θ = 10 deg. Working through the relationship above gives Radius (ρ) = 57.5877, x = 56.7128 and y = 10.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Radius (ρ) = 57.5877, x = 56.7128 and y = 10 should be roughly the size you expected from θ = 10 deg.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Angle, opening in degrees

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Cylindrical coordinates calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Checking a homework answer before you hand it in
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the x (Cartesian (x, y, z) to cylindrical (ρ, θ, z)), the y (Cartesian (x, y, z) to cylindrical (ρ, θ, z)) and the z (Cartesian (x, y, z) to cylindrical (ρ, θ, z)) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Cylindrical coordinates calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns z (Cylindrical (ρ, θ, z) to Cartesian (x, y, z)). The inputs are listed in the article. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Cylindrical coordinates calculator?
faq.a: The form has 6 fields, each listed with its unit in the article above. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter θ (Cartesian (x, y, z) to cylindrical (ρ, θ, z)) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Θ (Cartesian (x, y, z) to cylindrical (ρ, θ, z)) opens in degrees and the chip beside it offers 12 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Radius (ρ) = 57.5877. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Cylindrical coordinates calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
